about me

hi, I’m Yashi

I design things you touch and things you tap.

I’m a designer at SCAD studying Industrial Design with a focus on UX/UI. I like working on both sides: a watch for weightlifters one week, an office kiosk the next. Either way I start with the people using it and keep sketching until it feels obvious.

Design story

From Terminus to Tomorrow

Atlanta began as a railroad terminus and became a center of culture, business and innovation, just like AIG went from Shanghai to global. The building tells that story from the ground up.

“Every element embodies movement, honoring the past while embracing a future of progress and creativity.”

  • Wayfinding and room names from the oldest Atlanta neighborhoods to the newest
  • Collab walls that move from physical to digital
  • The mural in the stairs
  • Framed art, brief-based, by Atlanta artists
Wayfinding

A wayfinding formula

75% of people naturally rely on cardinal directions and mental maps in unfamiliar buildings, so every floor is split into quadrants named after landmarks in that direction.

Tap a quadrant
75%

rely on cardinal directions indoors

How it worksTap a quadrant on the plan. A room in Downtown’s SW quadrant is named after a Southwest Downtown landmark, so the name itself tells you where you are.

Distraction markers

Frosted glass, by neighborhood

Glass distraction markers keep meetings private and double as wayfinding: each floor’s pattern is drawn from its neighborhood.

West End, Wren’s Nest

Industrial Design, Forms & Brands

TERRA Collection

Fall 2025
Main RoleIndustrial Designer
Duration10 Weeks
TeamSolo
Project TypeConsumer Electronics × Agriculture
Meet the products →See 250 sketches →
The brief

Consumer electronics × agriculture

Consumer electronics make life easier. Agriculture gives us food. The brief asked for a product that brings the two together.

I flipped it around. Instead of putting electronics on the farm, Terra brings the honest, hands-first feel of farm tools into everyday home products: a massager, a hair dryer and a vacuum you start with a grip, a pull and a twist.

Designing products that feel grounded and dependable, blending purposeful mechanics with smooth, intuitive forms for a natural, effortless experience.

Brand research

Two industries, six brands

I started with a Forms & Brands study: three agriculture brands and three consumer-electronics brands, comparing visual DNA, form, color and materials. Pick an industry and a brand.

John Deere

Visual DNA
Bold, grounded, functional

Strength, trust, productivity

Form identity

  • Bulky wheels and treads
  • Trapezoid panels with softened edges
  • Curved hoods flowing into straight planes
  • Tall, upright cabins for visibility and authority

Materials

Steel chassis, sheet-metal and plastic hoods, rubber + steel wheels, ABS + glass cab

“The quality of our equipment… comes first, because the livelihood of farmers and ranchers quite literally depends on it.”John Deere

Kubota

Visual DNA
Vivid, compact, practical
Purpose
Efficiency, accessibility, modern progress

Form identity

  • Curved edges balanced by strong lines
  • High-visibility orange surfaces
  • Functional simplicity, no ornament
  • Operator-centred cab with clear sightlines

Materials

Cast steel and alloys, sheet metal, AR400 high-tensile steel, ceramic composites, rubber + polyurethane

“Customers seek new research and solutions. We will work to ensure that KUBOTA FARM is constantly evolving.”Kubota

“I’ve been using Mahindra tractors for over 10 years. They are reliable, sturdy, and get the job done.”Mahindra customer

From agriculture

Strength you can see: chunky, geometric volumes, high-visibility color and grippy, visible mechanics.

+
From electronics

Approachability: soft edges, minimal controls, calm neutrals and products that sit nicely in a home.

Terra

Tough, tactile tools for the home that start with one natural motion.

Market voice

What people say about them

Reviews and brand statements kept pointing to the same values: reliability, comfort and ease of use.

Competitors

Competitive position

Terra sits between John Deere’s rugged reliability and Dyson’s engineered precision. Drag the slider to see the blend.

TerraPurposeful, intuitive, built for lasting performance
RuggedRefined
Primary research

Survey: 42 people

I surveyed 42 people, from farmers and landscapers to students, about how devices should feel in the hand.

Q1

Which physical action feels most satisfying to start a device?

Twist a dial
38%
Squeeze / grip
29%
Pull a lever
21%
Press a button
12%

Twist, grip and pull beat buttons. That gave Terra three “verbs”, one per product.

Q2

What frustrates you most about handheld home devices?

Hidden or tiny controls
64%
Slippery grip
52%
Too many buttons
45%
Feels flimsy
40%

People want controls they can find without looking, and a grip that feels secure.

Q3

Which color pairing feels “durable but friendly”?

Orange + charcoal
41%
Green + charcoal
33%
All white
15%
All black
11%

Field-machine colors read as tough, but still warm. Orange and green won.

Q4

Would a product that looks like a tool feel trustworthy at home?

Yes
57%
Only if it still looks refined
36%
No
7%

The sweet spot: John Deere’s strength, refined with Dyson-level finish.

Primary research

Interviews

Four conversations, two with people who use tools for a living and two everyday users, about the moments a product feels right in your hand.

R

Ray, 58

Farmer, 30+ years
“My sprayer, my pump, my mower: I never look at them. My hands just know where everything is.”

Tools are learned through the hands, not the eyes.

D

Dana, 31

Landscaper
“I’d trust a gadget more if it felt like my gear. Heavy, grippy, nothing that rattles.”

Weight and texture signal quality more than looks.

P

Priya, 22

Design student, apartment renter
“My hair dryer has four tiny buttons and I still never know which setting I’m on.”

One clear motion should do one clear thing.

M

Marcus, 44

Parent, home gardener
“The vacuum is always buried in a closet because it’s a pain to set up.”

Instant start matters more than extra features.

Principles

Design principles

Everything I learned boiled down to four rules for the whole collection.

01Honest

Looks straightforward, showing how it works without being overly complicated.

02Earthy

Colors feel calm and grounded, never flashy or aggressive.

03Grippable

Textures that make it easy to hold, even with wet or tired hands.

04Consistent

The design feels the same from every angle and across all three products.

Interaction-focused design

Products respond naturally to grip, twist, press or rotation, inspired by sprayers, pumps and levers.

Squeeze the handle like a field sprayer and Terra Pulse switches on. No button to hunt for.

Pull the handle down like a mechanical lever and Terra Flow powers on.

Turn the central knob like a water valve and Terra Sweep starts instantly.

User testing

Eight people, three foam products, two rounds.

Testers held unlabelled foam models and had to start, hold and adjust them with no instructions. I watched where their hands went first, timed each task and asked them to think out loud. Then I changed the models and tested again.

8Participants
5Tasks each
2Rounds
96%Success in round 2
Find how to turn it on (no instructions)
50%
Hold for 2 minutes comfortably
63%
Swap a Pulse attachment
38%
Tell which way the Sweep knob turns
25%
Rate it “tough but friendly” (4–5/5)
50%
Finding 1

Handle was too thick

Small-handed testers couldn’t wrap their fingers around the first Pulse foam model.

ChangeSlimmed the grip from ~38 mm to ~32 mm and angled it 15° like a sprayer trigger.

Finding 2

Grooves felt sharp

Hand-cut grooves pressed into palms after a minute.

ChangeRounded every rib in clay and widened the spacing for a softer, still-grippy feel.

Finding 3

Attachments got mixed up

People couldn’t tell the four massage heads apart at a glance.

ChangeGave each head a distinct silhouette: ball, star, ribbed cylinder and wedge.

Finding 4

Knob direction unclear

On Sweep, 6 of 8 testers turned the knob the wrong way first.

ChangeAdded a raised notch and a faceted geometric knob so the rotation reads by touch.

“I didn’t even think about it. I just grabbed it and it worked, like picking up a garden sprayer.”
Round 2 participant, landscaper
Final product

The Terra collection

Three products, three natural motions, one family. Pick a product, follow the arrows, then try the control.

TerraPulse

Feel the strength. Control the comfort.

A handheld massager that activates as soon as it’s held, mimicking the “grip and use” action of agricultural sprayers. A compact body with a textured handle keeps it secure and stable.

Material
Rough plastic, silicone
Color language

TerraFlow

Rotate. Twist. Style.

A hair dryer that powers on when the handle is pulled down: a “pull to start” action borrowed from mechanical tools. Rotating the dial smoothly increases airflow, from focused styling to gentle drying.

Material
Rough plastic, metal
Color language

TerraSweep

Built strong. Works smooth.

A handheld vacuum that starts the moment its central knob is rotated, combining power and control in one intuitive motion.

Material
Rough plastic, metal
Color language
Color language
Terra Orange#FF8B1AEnergy and warmth, like field machinery
Field Green#8BC34AGrowth, freshness, comfort
Charcoal#2B2B2BMatte, durable, hides wear

My role

Solo industrial designer: brand research across six companies, a 42-person survey, interviews, 250 sketches, twelve foam models, two rounds of user testing, the Terra identity, and final CAD renders of Pulse, Flow and Sweep.

What I learned

The best interactions came from watching hands, not reading answers. Testers trusted the models that started with one honest motion, and every change after testing was about making that motion easier to feel.

Industrial Design, Lighting

Aerolicht

Fall 2025
Main RoleIndustrial Designer
TeamSolo
Inspired ByLuigi Colani
Project TypeInteractive Table Lamp
Rotate the lamp →See the wiring →
∀eroLICHT

The brief

Aerolicht is a rotatable, shell-structured table lamp that dims and brightens through its overlapping segments.

Brief

Design a lamp inspired by the philosophy of one designer. Mine was Luigi Colani.

Goal

Translate his biodynamic, nature-led thinking into a physical object, not just copy his look.

Deliverables

Research, ideation sketches, form models, a working prototype and a presentation with brand and brochure.

Designer study: Luigi Colani

A German industrial designer of futuristic, organic, aerodynamic objects, and the philosophy the lamp had to answer to.

  1. 1928Born in BerlinGerman industrial designer, later known worldwide.
  2. ParisStudied aerodynamicsThe science of flow became the root of his forms.
  3. 1950sCarsDesigned for Fiat, Alfa Romeo, Lancia, Volkswagen and BMW.
  4. CaliforniaMcDonnell DouglasWorked in aerospace before moving into products.
  5. WorldwideEverything elseFurniture, product and environmental design around the world.
“

The earth is round, all the heavenly bodies are round. Why should I join the straying mass who want to make everything angular? My world is also round.

Luigi Colani

Biodynamic thinking

His forms were rounded, organic and, in his word, biodynamic. He looked to nature first and believed those forms were ergonomically superior.

“I look at the shark and its shape: 140 million years without change. Is that success? Look at birds, look at fish. Things that look good, work good.”Luigi Colani

Precedent analysis

Three projects that show how he moved the same thinking from cars to furniture.

19601,700+units soldColani GT kit car

The world’s first series-produced kit car, built on a Volkswagen Beetle chassis. Over 1,700 units sold.

19631stplastic monocoqueBMW 700 plastic monocoque

The first plastic monocoque sports car. A prototype that proved new materials and biodynamic shapes.

1960s4furniture brandsFurniture for Asko, Fritz Hansen, COR and Kusch+Co

Pieces like the Körperform chairs took his ergonomic, curved forms into homes.

Form studies

Sketching over his chairs, seating and piano to learn how his curves carry weight and invite the body. Tap a board to enlarge.

Design criteria

Four principles from the research. Every concept was judged against them.

  1. 01Organic formNo hard corners. Continuous curves from base to shade.Rejection of conventional design
  2. 02Borrowed from natureA structure that reads as scales, feathers or a shell.Nature as inspiration
  3. 03FlowElements layered in one direction, like an aerodynamic surface.Efficiency and aerodynamics
  4. 04Hand-led interactionLight controlled by touching the form, not a hidden switch.Ergonomics and human-centered design

Ideation and quick models

Seven directions explored in sketches and fast models in paper, foil, clay and acrylic, each with a different way for light to escape.

  1. 01Folded leafLight tucked inside a folded petal.
  2. 02TriangleA flat triangle with light glowing from one corner.
  3. 03Diamond eyeA long diamond frame with a radial light at its center.
  4. 04Rolled formA soft roll with slits that emit light.
  5. 05Cork boardA hexagon panel with a moving light bar.
  6. 06Clay triangleMolded clay with light emitted toward small hooks.
  7. 07Petal clusterA flower of panels around a center light. Press down to release.

Concept selection

Shells on a wooden ring moved forward.

Hits all four criteria

Round ring, shell layering, one flowing direction and a touch-driven way to dim.

The light is the interaction

Rotating the shells changes how much light escapes, so dimming is part of the form.

Buildable in the shop

Wood, acrylic, wire and clay: materials and processes I could prototype at full scale.

Concept sketch

The chosen direction, annotated for light, material, structure and movement.

  • LED lightRuns along the inside of the top shell.
  • ShadowEach shell casts a soft edge onto the next.
  • Made with acrylicFrosted shells diffuse the light.
  • Wire placementA wire spine holds the shells in a curve.
  • Joints and heavy pointsMolded with clay where the weight sits.
  • Rotates to dim and lightenThe shells travel along the wooden ring.

Mechanism: rotate to dim

The shells ride along the ring. Closed, they overlap and hold the light in; opened, they fan out and let it spill. Drag the dial to try it.

80%
Light color
Room

Component breakdown

Six parts working as one gesture. Tap a number.

  1. 1
    LED on the back of the top shellThe light source sits under the first shell, so you never see the bulb.
  2. 2
    Frosted acrylic shellsSeven shells, each smaller than the last, overlap to diffuse the light.
  3. 3
    Wire spine and hooksA bent wire connects the shells and controls their angle.
  4. 4
    Clay-molded jointsAcrylic was too heavy on its own, so the heavy points got molded joints.
  5. 5
    Wooden ring standA strong, stable base for the rotating light mechanism.
  6. 6
    Rotates to dim and brightenTurning the shells along the ring opens or closes the light.

Materials

Each material was picked for one job.

Ring standWood

Warm, structural base, shaped into one continuous ring with a flat foot.

Seven shellsFrosted acrylic

Diffuses the light into a soft glow and hides the source.

Spine and hooksSteel wire

Threads through every shell and sets each one’s angle.

JointsClay

Molded at the heavy points to carry the weight of the acrylic.

Light sourceColor LEDs

Mounted under the top shell. Warm white plus color modes.

Prototyping and iteration

The full-scale build showed what the sketches couldn’t: weight.

  1. 01HookThe top of the spine hooks onto the ring.
  2. 02Wire to connectOne wire threads through every shell.
  3. 03Acrylic shellsFrosted acrylic shaped into seven shells.
  4. 04Wires bent to control the acrylicBending the wire sets each shell’s angle.
  5. 05Acrylic is too heavy, so I had to put jointsClay joints spread the load at the heavy points.
Iteration 1Shells hung on wire hooks

The acrylic shells were too heavy for the wire alone. They sagged and lost their layered angle.

→
Iteration 2Molded clay joints

I added clay joints at every heavy point so the wire holds each shell at its angle while it still rotates.

Wiring

I wired the lamp myself. Every routing decision answers one Colani rule: the form stays one continuous body, so the power has to disappear inside it. Press power, then tap a step.

  1. 1
    Power in at the footThe cord enters low at the back of the flat base, where the lamp already meets the table.Why, after ColaniColani hid mechanics so the form reads as one body. A cord at the base is the least visible exit, and the weight keeps it planted.
  2. 2
    Hidden channel in the ringThe wire travels inside the wooden ring along its seam instead of running along the outside.Why, after ColaniNo exposed lines on the surface. The ring stays a pure, uninterrupted curve, the way he treated car bodies as one skin.
  3. 3
    Following the curveThe run bends with the ring rather than taking the shortest straight path.Why, after Colani“My world is also round.” Even the wire follows the organic line; nothing inside the lamp is angular either.
  4. 4
    Out through the top jointThe wire leaves the ring where the first shell is joined, so the joint hides the exit.Why, after ColaniJoints carry both weight and power, the way his forms combined structure and function in one element.
  5. 5
    LED under the top shellThe LEDs sit on the underside of the largest shell. The frosted acrylic diffuses them into one soft glow.Why, after ColaniLight that seems to come from inside the form, like a living thing, never a bare bulb.
ConcealedNo wire is visible on the finished lamp.
CurvedEvery run follows the ring’s geometry.
ServiceableThe exit at the joint keeps the LED reachable.
Light from withinThe source is hidden behind frosted acrylic.

Final prototype

Lights off and lights on.

Brand: Vero Licht

A small lighting brand built for the presentation: logo, four brochure cards and printed renders.

The Aerolicht’s shell-like structure embodies Luigi Colani’s biodynamic design, favoring curved, organic forms over angular ones. Its rotational dimming is an interactive, sculptural approach to light control, typical of his futuristic aesthetic.
The lamp’s wooden stand provides strength and stability, acting as a robust foundation for the rotating light mechanism.
Aerolicht is a rotatable, shell-structured lamp that dims and brightens light through its overlapping segments, offering versatile, atmospheric illumination.
Organic, fluid form and functional movement reflect Luigi Colani’s biomorphic design philosophy, blending nature, art, and ergonomics.

How Colani shows up

The four criteria, answered in the final lamp.

Rejection of conventional designRound, never angular

A continuous wooden ring with a flat base. No corners anywhere.

Nature as inspirationShells like scales and feathers

Overlapping shells borrow from fish scales, feathers and pine cones.

Efficiency and aerodynamicsLayered like a fin

The shells stack in one flowing direction, like an aerodynamic surface.

Ergonomics and human-centered designLight you control by hand

Rotate the shells to dim or brighten. No switch to find.

Silent voice becomes visible

SLAYT is an enchanted learning companion for classrooms. It lets students silently communicate comprehension, confusion, or how they feel through touch-based interactions. It empowers shy, anxious, or neurodiverse learners to participate without fear of judgment, while giving teachers real-time insight into how the whole class is doing.

Problem

In most classrooms, the only way to show you understand is to raise your hand and speak. Quiet, anxious, ESL and neurodiverse students often know the answer but stay silent, so teachers read silence as confusion and the students who need support most stay invisible.

Solution

A desk-sized device with four shape buttons, a mood slider and a stylus screen. Students answer and check in privately; the teacher sees an anonymized, real-time picture of the whole class on a dashboard.

Challenge

Design a way for students to participate without speaking, and for teachers to see understanding as it happens.

My Role

Everything but the film: research, sketching, CAD, Arduino prototyping, UX flows and the teacher dashboard.

Outcome

A working Arduino prototype, a 3D-printed housing, a teacher dashboard and a “because every voice deserves to be heard” film.

Because every voice deserves to be heard.

SLAYT turns invisible emotions and understanding into visible, respectful signals. It doesn’t demand attention and it never singles anyone out. Like a thoughtful friend who notices when someone understands but hesitates to speak.

Who is it for?

SLAYT is designed for students aged 5–13 who hesitate to speak up because of shyness, anxiety, language barriers, or fear of being wrong.

Research

How I learned why quiet students stay quiet, and what teachers actually need to know.

1Method

Classroom observation

Watching how often quiet students actually speak up, and what happens when a teacher asks “Does everyone get it?”

2Method

Teacher interviews

How teachers read the room today, and what they wish they knew in the moment.

3Method

Student survey

How comfortable students feel answering out loud, and what would make it easier.

4Method

Competitive scan

Clickers, Kahoot, hand signals and exit tickets. All of them put answers on a public screen or come too late.

“

Teachers assume silence means confusion.

Key insight, from research

How might we let students show understanding without asking them to speak?

How might we give teachers a real-time read of the room without singling anyone out?

Value Proposition

Telepathy: human-to-human connection

SLAYT enables silent communication between students and teachers. Students don’t need to speak, raise hands, or expose themselves publicly to be understood. It creates a form of classroom “telepathy”, letting understanding, confusion, or readiness reach the teacher instantly and silently.

What’s enchanted

It connects human emotion and intention with technology in a way that feels natural, supportive, and invisible.

Personas

One for the student, one for the device itself, so every design decision had a personality to answer to.

AA

Aarav, 11

Suburban public school, class of 30

A thoughtful, observant student who enjoys learning but feels uncomfortable speaking in front of the class. He often knows the answer, but the fear of saying something wrong, or being laughed at, keeps his hand down.

Goals

  • Participate without drawing attention
  • Show understanding without speaking
  • Feel included and confident in class
  • Avoid embarrassment or judgment

Frustrations

  • Anxiety when asked to speak publicly
  • Fear of being wrong in front of peers
  • Teachers assuming silence means confusion
  • Feeling invisible despite understanding

Behaviors

  • Avoids raising hand even when confident
  • Listens carefully and takes notes
  • Engages more in written work than discussion
  • Participates when called on privately

Needs

  • A low-pressure way to communicate understanding
  • Privacy while participating
  • Reassurance that understanding is recognized
  • Control over when and how to interact
S

SLAYT

Core purpose

The kind of presence that doesn’t demand attention but never misses a moment. Empathetic, patient and reassuring. It exists to reduce anxiety, not add to it, and to create space for participation without pressure.

Personality

  • Empathetic
  • Calm
  • Observant
  • Supportive
  • Non-judgmental

Physical

  • Desk-sized and non-intrusive
  • Soft, rounded form
  • Touch-responsive surface
  • Subtle ambient glow
  • Silent operation (no sound alerts)

Behavior

  • Waits patiently for interaction
  • Responds instantly but gently
  • Never draws public attention to a student
  • Reflects collective mood, not individuals
  • Powers down quietly when not in use

Functional

  • Accepts touch inputs
  • Confirms input with gentle feedback
  • Sends anonymized data wirelessly
  • Aggregates class understanding in real time

How it works

Four ways to speak without speaking. Tap a feature.

Four shape buttons

Circle, triangle, square, diamond. Each maps to a multiple-choice answer, so students can respond to the teacher’s question without saying a word. Shape plus color also works for color-blind students.

Mood slider

A physical slider on the side: happy, okay, or lost. Students can show how well they understand the lesson right now, and the teacher sees the class average, never a single name.

Question display

The LCD mirrors the teacher’s question in real time, so every student reads it at their own pace instead of hearing it once.

Note-taking screen

A stylus canvas for working out the problem and capturing key points, with undo, redo, clear and zoom on the side rail.

My Role

I led SLAYT end to end: research, sketching, CAD and rendering, Arduino prototyping, UX flows and the teacher dashboard. The film was made with Motion Media students.

What I learned

Silence doesn’t mean confusion, and the quietest students often have the answer. Designing for them meant making every input private, physical and instant, and giving teachers a read of the room without putting anyone on the spot. Building it in hardware also taught me to test the feel of a button as seriously as the flow of a screen.

SPYDR is a performance-driven watch combining precision and strength: palm-secure bands that stabilize grip and track power, built for athletes pushing boundaries in weightlifting and endurance training.

The problem

Most watches stop at the wrist

Normal smartwatches put every sensor under the watch body. They count steps well, but can’t tell how hard you’re gripping a bar, whether both sides are pulling evenly, or when you’re fatiguing. I started by auditing what today’s wearables get wrong.

01Discomfort & fit

Bands irritate skin or feel loose during long wear.

02Screen visibility

Small display, hard to read in bright light or mid-movement.

03Charging

Chargers are inconvenient and easy to misplace.

04Battery life

Frequent charging interrupts training.

05Complexity

Menus are confusing, especially for older adults.

06Data overload

Too much data, not personalized or actionable.

Task analysis, checking heart rate
  1. 1Lift wrist
  2. 2Screen wakes
  3. 3Navigate to heart-rate
  4. 4Wait for reading
  5. 5Read value
  6. 6Interpret zone

6 steps, small text. Redesign: the device should push the number to you, with an automatic notification or buzz, instead of making you dig for it.

Competitors
Apple Watch

Best ecosystem + features, but expensive and heavy.

Garmin

Excellent for athletes, rugged, but bulky.

Whoop

Recovery and sleep focus, but subscription-based.

Fitbit

Affordable and light, but little personalization or comfort.

Opportunity: a comfortable, accessible wearable made for strength, not steps.

Anthropometrics

Designing for every wrist

Wrist circumference ranges from about 140 mm (5th percentile female) to 210 mm (95th percentile male). Drag to see how the band adapts.

175 mm50th percentile
140 mm210 mm
  • Band: 8.3" (211 mm) full length covers the full range with stretch
  • Strap width: < 20 mm for small wrists, > 24 mm for large
  • Screen: 30–40 mm diagonal for glance readability
  • Button / haptic zone: 25–30 mm from the wrist edge, within thumb reach

Fits, straps at 50% stretch

Material test

Can a soft band hold a sensor under load?

Before committing to rubber straps, I made clay strips at different thicknesses and pressed them between my palm and a dumbbell, starting at 5 lb and working up. A second participant tested heavier deadlift loads.

Clay held its shape at every thickness. Even the thinnest strip stayed in place across the palm.

Result: a rubber or silicone band can securely hold embedded sensors under heavy lifting, as long as thickness and sensor placement are optimized.

Ideation

Sketching the fit

Ideas ranged from grip-back cuffs and twin wrist pods to a glove with sensor seams and a “spider-limb” watch that slides through the palm. Follow the arrows.

Concepts

Three concepts

I developed three directions to test with real lifts: the SPYDR Watch, a Smart Glove and a Dual Wrist Band. Each got orthographic drawings and a feature spec.

SPYDR Watch

A round 1.2" screen held by four straps that cross the palm and wrap the wrist. Sensors live in the straps, not just under the watch.

  • Pressure / tension sensors in each strap detect how much force is applied
  • Measures grip strength and dynamic tension to show fatigue
  • Back sensor for heart rate, bioimpedance and skin temperature
  • Straight fit or criss-cross fit for extra anchoring

Smart Glove

A fingerless glove with sensor seams along the index finger and thumb, a power button at the wrist and breathable cotton sides.

  • Grip sensors along index and thumb
  • Heavy-duty / industrial nitrile thickness (6–8 mil)
  • One size fits all using stretch fabrics
  • Digital watch back in silicone

Dual Wrist Band

A 1.2 × 1.6" screen on two stretchable rubber bands, with a gap between them for ventilation and sensors.

  • Two bands for extra support and grip
  • Wearable on the wrist or looped around the thumb
  • Sensors track direction, muscle activity and heart rate
  • On/off and move buttons on the side
Two ways to wear SPYDR

Straight fit

Straps go straight across: simpler data tracking, everyday use, and symmetric force measurement.

The first wearable model: a watch body with four red straps and taped buckles, tested straight on my hand to check where the straps should cross the palm.

All three concepts, built and worn: the palm-crossing watch, the dual band and two glove versions in fabric and nitrile.

Black silicone straps, molded buckle clips and a working sensor strip with indicator LEDs. Follow the arrows.

Heuristics

Heuristic evaluation

I scored all three against Nielsen’s ten heuristics, adapted for physical products. Open a row to see what testers did and what it taught me.

HeuristicSPYDRGloveDual
Visibility of system statusHighHighModerate

SPYDR: The design looked active, but it wasn’t always clear how to wear it or which side was correct.

→ Physical design should make orientation and wearability clear without instructions.

Match with the real worldHighModerateHigh

SPYDR: The crossed straps followed muscle and tendon lines naturally. It felt connected to real hand movement.

→ The closer a design feels to existing workout gear, the faster people understand it.

User control & freedomLowLowModerate

SPYDR: Tight straps made it hard to adjust once on.

→ Allow fast adjustments with one hand mid-session.

Consistency & standardsHighHighLow

SPYDR: Straps and sensor areas looked integrated, creating a consistent look.

→ Uniform design and fit build trust and comfort during use.

Error preventionModerateLowLow

SPYDR: Could be worn the wrong way if users didn’t notice the strap direction.

→ Design should visually guide correct wear: small icons or color cues.

Recognition over recallHighModerateModerate

SPYDR: Once seen, users remembered how it wrapped because of its unique shape.

→ Clear shapes and recognizable patterns improve reuse.

Flexibility & efficiencyHighLowHigh

SPYDR: Fit different arm sizes but needed readjusting between users.

→ Materials should stretch and adapt without losing structure.

Aesthetic & minimalistLowLowLow

SPYDR: Futuristic, strong visual identity. Some found the “spider” shape intimidating.

→ A lighter, minimal form reads as more comfortable and professional.

Recover from errorsModerateLowLow

SPYDR: Hard to notice if straps were twisted until already tightened.

→ Clear markings or directional materials reduce setup errors.

Help & documentationModerateLowModerate

SPYDR: Didn’t need much guidance but could use icons to show fit direction.

→ Even intuitive designs benefit from small molded cues for first-time users.

Key insight

SPYDR was the most accurate for muscle-tension analysis, but its feedback scored lowest.

The Dual Band won on comfort, the Glove on grip measurement, but SPYDR’s strap sensors gave the best data. The problem wasn’t the hardware. People couldn’t see or feel what it was telling them mid-lift: the watch face wasn’t visible, buttons were too small to press, and no one knew when it was working.

2.5Feedback clarity↓So I designed the interface.
Part two, UX

An interface you can use with a barbell in your hands

A lifting watch can’t behave like a phone on your wrist. Mid-set your hands are full, you’re breathing hard, and the screen is moving. I designed SPYDR OS around those human factors, then tested it with the same five people.

Requirements

From test findings to requirements

Every interface decision traces back to something a tester said. Pick a finding.

Haptics first

Every key event has a vibration pattern, so you never need to look mid-rep.

Constraints

Human factors on a 1.2-inch screen

The rules that every screen had to pass.

1 s

Glance budget

Mid-set information must be readable in under a second. Rep count fills ~55% of the screen.

30 mm

Screen (1.2")

Round face, so content sits in the center 70% and the outer ring carries status.

≥ 9 mm

Touch targets

Sweaty, chalky fingers: only 2–3 targets per screen, each at least 9 mm.

7:1

Contrast

White on true black for OLED: readable under gym lights and saves battery.

0

Touches mid-set

Reps, tempo and form are detected by the strap sensors, so hands stay on the bar.

4

Haptic patterns

A small, learnable vocabulary instead of dozens of buzzes.

My role

Solo industrial and UX designer: wearable research and benchmarking, anthropometrics, clay material tests, sketching, three concepts with orthographic drawings, low- and high-fidelity prototypes, two rounds of usability testing, and the SPYDR OS watch interface.

What I learned

Testing showed the product wasn’t failing on hardware but on feedback. For something worn mid-lift, the best interface is often not the screen at all. It’s a buzz you can feel and a single number you can read in a second.

VAERS Reimagined

Quickly know what we did!

A 10-week SCADpro studio with Deloitte asked one question: how do we make vaccine safety reporting accessible, intuitive, and trustworthy for everyone? With patients, caregivers, and clinicians in mind, we built a full ecosystem: an outreach campaign, a modern responsive platform, a friendly AI guide named VERA, and clinician tools that live inside Epic and MyChart.

PatientCaregiverClinician

Problem

VAERS only learns about adverse events when someone files a report, and underreporting is its biggest limitation. Most people have never heard of it, the form is long and full of medical jargon, and clinicians don’t have time to re-enter data they already charted.

Solution

We reimagined VAERS as a connected experience instead of a one-off form: plain-language guided reporting, multi-language support, Quick and Responsive form paths, an always-available chatbot, Epic/MyChart auto-fill for clinicians, and a campaign that reaches people before they ever need to report.

Challenge

Reimagine VAERS reporting to be accessible, intuitive, and trustworthy for patients, caregivers, and clinicians.

My Role

UX Strategy: research, interviews, survey, journey mapping, and opportunity framing.

Outcome

Report time cut ~85% in testing. Delivered a platform, a campaign, and an ecosystem to Deloitte.

VAERS is only as strong as the reports it receives.

Co-sponsored by the CDC and FDA, VAERS is the nation’s early warning system for vaccine safety. But its front end hasn’t kept pace. The current form dates back to the 2017 VAERS 2.0 rollout, with cluttered tables, inconsistent hierarchy, and no responsive design.

HHS says it plainly: “Underreporting is one of the main limitations of passive surveillance systems, including VAERS.” Every report that goes unfiled is a signal the system never sees.

To begin, we needed to understand why people weren’t reporting, and what would make reporting feel worth doing.

38survey respondents
3stakeholder groups interviewed
5personas
4client reviews with Deloitte
3user paths prototyped
~85%faster reporting

People are willing to report. They don’t know VAERS exists, and when they find it, the form takes too long.

Listening First

We built empathy maps for clinicians, caregivers, and the public, then interviewed each group. Their answers changed how we saw the problem.

Says

“I trust my doctor completely.”

“I didn’t know there was a place to report these things.”

“I usually just wait for symptoms to go away.”

The doctor is the gatekeeper.

Does

Feels

Overwhelmed and uncertain, but safety matters more to them than privacy.

“

Yes, absolutely.

Caregiver, asked if they’d report now that they know VAERS exists
“

When you’re on a busy shift, it’s overwhelming to pull information together.

Clinician, on reporting barriers
“

I’m not originally from the United States, and I have some trouble understanding medical terms.

Parent, on reporting to a government platform

The caregiver’s answer reframed the project: the barrier isn’t willingness, it’s awareness. For clinicians it’s time. For parents reading medical English as a second language, jargon is a double barrier.

Competitor Interface Patterns

We analyzed public health and wellness platforms to understand where VAERS falls behind and where it can lead.

VAERS

Official and trusted, but dense tables, weak hierarchy, and not mobile-friendly.

Strength: Trust
V-safe

Strength: Speed
headspace

Strength: Calm
TraceTogether

A national tool that earned public trust through clarity and quick recognition.

Strength: Clarity

Illustration as support

Graphics explain, they don’t decorate. Photography adds warmth next to text.

One consistent system

Icons, line weights, and color stay the same everywhere, so recognition is instant.

Calm, restrained color

Soft, muted palettes signal safety. Text contrast stays near 7:1 for readability.

Design Principles

01

Plain Language First

Medical jargon becomes words a worried parent would use. Clinicians still get standardized terms when they need them.

02

Guide, Don’t Demand

Progressive disclosure shows only the fields that matter, with a progress bar so no one feels lost.

03

Fit the Workflow

For clinicians, VAERS lives inside Epic and MyChart, not in another tab they have to remember.

04

Every Language Counts

Multi-language support and reading-level options let every family report with the same confidence.

05

Close the Loop

Every report ends with a confirmation that explains what happens next and why it mattered.

06

Accessible by Default

7:1 text contrast, generous white space, and streamlined graphics, in line with Section 508.

From a Form to an Ecosystem

Three opportunities kept coming up: lack of education, lack of trust, and no incentive. So we designed a system that works before, during, and after a report.

1
Caregiver

Clear language, guided reporting

Reduce hesitation at the very first step.

2
Clinician

Seamless integration into healthcare workflow

Report where the data already lives.

3
Patient

Multi-language, jargon-free guidance

Anyone can report with confidence.

Finding the Visual Language

We explored three stylescapes and let users decide. Over half chose Friendly & Photographic, a third chose Clinical & Minimal. So we combined them: real people inside a clean, credible interface.

Visual design survey, 38 responses. Final direction: Confidence Care photography inside Clinical Clarity’s clean structure.

Clinic White#F6F7F6
Night Shift Navy#030526
Booster Blue#26418F
Scrub Teal#76ADBB
Healthy Green#90BB5A
Immunity Yellow#F8D768

Visual Tone

Built from CDC color guidance. Booster Blue for trust, Healthy Green for progress, Immunity Yellow for reassurance. Photography shows real people so users see themselves in the experience.

Interaction Cues

Clear button states and progress indicators confirm every action. Icons and color carry the hierarchy so each page can be scanned at a glance.

Meet VERA

Our AI guide needed a face that was friendly but still trustworthy. We tested three directions, and the vaccine bottle won by a landslide.

Vaccine BottleWinner

Soft, supportive, clear
65.4%

Instantly tied to vaccine safety, and neutral across gender, race, and age.

Nurse Assistant

Empathetic, human
23.1%

Warm and reassuring, but less specific to what VAERS does.

V

V Symbol

Neutral, structured
11.5%

Clean and professional, but users wanted something more personal.

72%enjoy VAERS having a mascot
89%are open to an AI chatbot guide
11%said no to a mascot. Low resistance for a health tool.

VERA lives in the chat, onboarding, and help moments, exactly where users are most likely to hesitate. She answers questions in plain language, on every page.

Key Design Decisions

The work changed a lot between reviews. These are the calls that shaped the final product, and why we made them.

01

Mascot direction
First idea

VERA as a Band-Aid character.

What we learned

It didn’t land with clinicians or the public at check-in.

Decision

Explored 3 new directions and let users vote. The vaccine bottle won with 65.4%.

02

Visual style
First idea

Pick one of three stylescapes.

What we learned

Users wanted warmth (51.4%) but also credibility (32.4%).

Decision

Combined Confidence Care’s photography with Clinical Clarity’s clean layout.

03

Site structure
First idea

Five top-level sections organized around the system.

What we learned

Reporting was buried two levels deep, and Follow-Up was separated from it.

Decision

Three sections by user goal: Report, About VAERS, Vaccine Information.

04

Form order
First idea

Patient details first: 13 questions before anything about the reaction.

What we learned

People come to describe what happened. Personal questions up front felt like a wall.

Decision

Lead with vaccine, symptoms, and severity. Ask identity later, and review before submitting.

05

Form entry point
First idea

One form for everyone.

What we learned

Patients, caregivers, and clinicians struggled in different sections.

Decision

Three tailored paths, plus Quick and Responsive forms for different confidence levels.

06

Clinician experience
First idea

A faster mobile form for clinicians.

What we learned

Clinicians were less confident in VAERS than we assumed, and they already chart in Epic.

Decision

Epic/MyChart auto-fill, a Quick Form fallback, and a desktop version.

07

Human vs. AI help
First idea

A chatbot for all support.

What we learned

89% were open to AI, but caregivers like Marcus preferred a real person.

Decision

VERA on every page, with a Get Support option to reach a live representative.

Built for a 14-Minute Visit

14min

That’s the average time a clinician spends with each patient, while already documenting everything in Epic. Asking them to type it all again into VAERS is the burden. So we brought VAERS to them.

1

Capture + sync

Vaccination data syncs across Epic and MyChart.

2

Detect + pre-fill

Symptoms are flagged and a VAERS report is auto-filled.

3

Review + submit

Patient, vaccine, and symptom timeline in one view. Submit without leaving the workflow.

Quick Report fallback

When systems can’t share data, a Quick Form lets clinicians paste patient details into a streamlined structure. Symptoms use standardized medical terms in an alphabetical dropdown for faster, more accurate reports. A summary screen verifies everything before direct submission.

A front door people understand

Responsive form: one question at a time

Healthcare provider quick report

Built for one hand

Full-width buttons, large tap targets, and one decision per screen.

Always know where you are

A four-step progress bar (Patient, Vaccine, Symptoms, Submit) on every form screen.

Nothing is a dead end

Skip, edit any past answer, or ask VERA, at every step.

Next Steps

What we’d validate if the project continued.

Test the hi-fi flows

Run usability tests on the final screens with caregivers and non-native English speakers.

Prove the integration

Work with Deloitte engineers to confirm Epic/MyChart data exchange and privacy requirements.

Measure the campaign

My Role

I was on the Strategy Team, working with our strategy lead and the creative team. Our team turned the research into the direction for the redesign: who reports, where they get stuck, and what a simpler form needed to do.

What I learned

A government form is still an experience, and most of the friction lives in what the form asks before it asks anything useful. Working on strategy taught me to design the decision first and the screen second, and to back every change with something real users told us.

A screen that turns waiting into wayfinding

AIG × SCADpro brought digital and physical touchpoints together in AIG’s new Atlanta office. On the digital side, our team focused on the elevator lobby: a wall-mounted kiosk that helps employees find and book rooms, see what’s happening at AIG and around Atlanta, and meet coworkers in the minute they spend waiting for the elevator.

Context

The ask

Design interactive experiences for AIG’s new Atlanta office. We zeroed in on the elevator lobby, a place everyone passes through several times a day, where time is short and people are already deciding where to go next.

Every floor’s elevator lobby is a high-traffic transition point.
Research

Navigation is really decision-making

When we lined up the team’s interviews and observations, a pattern showed up: the problem wasn’t only finding your way. It was deciding what to do next while on the move. Hover each card.

01A decision problem, not a wayfinding onePeople don’t just need directions. They need to see what’s available and what to do next, fast.
02Time pressure amplifies frictionFrustration spikes in the gaps between meetings and floors: short, high-pressure moments with no time to explore.
03Low visibility creates hesitationIt was hard to tell which rooms were free, what was happening in the building, or who to talk to.

What I learned

Reflection

This project got me excited about designing systems that support people in their everyday work.

1

Workflows are shaped by space, time and emotion, not just screens.

2

Clarity lowers stress and leads to better decisions.

3

Designing for a physical space means rethinking visibility, interaction time and flow compared to a normal app.

4

Bringing many stakeholders together surfaces gaps early and leads to more creative solutions.

The problem

Document-rich. Intelligence-poor.

That line ended up as the hero headline, because it describes the customer’s problem exactly. It also described the old site: lots of information, not much clarity, and a look that didn’t match a modern AI company.

6

Stakeholder interviews

CEO, sales, product, engineering and two client-success leads.

8

Buyer interviews

Claims, utilization review, TPA ops and IT compliance leaders.

4

Competitor audits

Document AI, claims AI, medical review and automation vendors.

12

Sales calls reviewed

Recorded demos, to hear the questions buyers really ask.

Key insights

What we heard

Four patterns came up again and again across interviews and sales calls.

01“What do you actually do?”

5 of 8 buyers couldn’t explain ATOM after reading the old homepage. Product names (Record Ranger, Agents, Connect) meant nothing without the bigger picture.

02Trust comes before features

Every buyer in healthcare and insurance asked about compliance and data storage before asking what the product does.

03“AI” is a red flag on its own

Buyers have been burned by pilots. They wanted to see where people stay in control, not more automation promises.

04Sales repeats the same story

The sales team drew the same ecosystem diagram on every call. The website should tell that story so calls can start further along.

Personas

Who the site is for

Three buyer personas, built from the interviews. Each one needed something different from the same page.

D

Dana, 46

VP of Claims Operations, Third-party administrator

“I don’t need another AI tool. I need to know it fits how my adjusters already work.”

Goals

  • Cut the time adjusters spend digging through files
  • Show leadership a clear ROI
  • Avoid another failed AI pilot

Frustrations

  • Every vendor says “AI”, none say how
  • Can’t tell products apart
  • Needs proof before a call

What the site must do

Understand, in under a minute, what ATOM does and where it fits in her claims workflow.

M

Marcus, 39

Director of Utilization Review, Health plan

“If a nurse can’t see why a field was filled in, we can’t use it.”

Goals

  • Faster prior-auth turnaround
  • Clinical staff stay in control
  • Traceable decisions for audits

Frustrations

  • Black-box automation
  • Accuracy claims with no backing
  • Long sales cycles to get basic answers

What the site must do

See accuracy, human review and source traceability explained plainly.

P

Priya, 35

IT Security & Compliance Lead, P&C carrier

“Where does our data live, and who keeps it? That’s my first question, every time.”

Goals

  • Vendor passes security review fast
  • No client data retained
  • Clear documentation

Frustrations

  • Compliance info hidden or missing
  • Vague answers about data storage
  • Has to email sales for basics

What the site must do

Find SOC2, HIPAA and data-retention answers without talking to anyone.

Concept exploration

Illustration concepts

Before the final diagrams, I sketched and rendered 3D concepts that explain each product as a physical object. Pick a product, then flip between my sketch and the render.

ATOM 3D, Discover, Design, Deploy

A magnifying glass over the workflow

ATOM 3D follows three steps: Discovery maps workflows and finds intelligence gaps, Design co-creates the future state, and Deploy puts the ecosystem in place. The lens and building blocks show “looking closely, then rebuilding with intention.”

Record Ranger OS, Document intelligence

A machine that turns paper into data

Record Ranger takes in any P&C or medical document, then classifies, extracts and summarizes it, with human review before delivering clean, structured output. Messy files go in one side and tidy blocks come out the other.

AI Agents, Activation

A core that plugs into your systems

Structured data flows from Record Ranger into custom agents that plug into existing systems and automate decisions end to end. The glass panels show the agent connecting to each tool, while the client keeps full ownership of the agent IP.

Interactive concept

Point to Point

One graphic for the whole ecosystem, mixing 3D and flat elements. Each part is a touchpoint visitors can click to watch a demo or learn about that step. It started as sketches of a messy workflow becoming organized, layered intelligence.

Starting from the logo

My first recommendation pulled straight from ATOM’s logo: a bright orange to drive action, a dark grey for a clean modern feel, and soft neutrals for backgrounds. Testing it against the healthcare and insurance audience pushed the final palette toward navy and blue for trust.

Findings → fixes

What changed

Each finding turned into a specific design change you can see on the live site.

Finding 1

“Where am I?”

People got lost moving between product pages.

Change: Added the “Four capabilities. One ecosystem.” card row to every product page, with a “You are here” state.

Finding 2

Trust was hard to find

Testers scrolled to the footer looking for security answers.

Change: Added a proof strip under heroes, compliance badges in the footer and a “Credibility is structural” block on About.

Finding 3

Too much jargon up top

The 5-second test failed on the first hero.

Change: Kept the bold “Document-rich. Intelligence-poor.” line but added a plain subline explaining the ecosystem.

Finding 4

Two CTAs competing

“Contact” and “Book Demo” pulled in different directions.

Change: One “Book Demo” button in the nav, and a quiet floating “Contact Us” tab.

Months 7–9

Phase 2: a sales demo system

After launch, I spent three months on the product side. An AI engineer had built the demo system the sales team used with clients. It worked, but it was hard to present. I redesigned it into a modern, guided demo that matches the new brand.

Months 1–6Rebrand + website, from scratch
Months 7–9Sales demo system modernization
01Audit the engineer’s build

Sat in on demos to see where the existing system confused clients or slowed sales down.

02Design a guided demo flow

03Apply the new brand

Brought the UI in line with the website, so the demo feels like the same company clients just read about.

My role

Solo UX/UI and brand designer on a 9-month full-time contract. I led the research, revamped the entire ATOM brand, designed the IA and every page, built the site in Wix, ran usability testing, and then modernized the sales demo system.

What I learned

With a technical product, structure does most of the explaining. Once the navigation matched the product’s own story, the copy could get shorter and the pages got clearer. Being the only designer also taught me to back decisions with research, not taste.

Quickly know what we did!

This 10-week project with 30+ designers asked: what should the future of Porsche’s EV interiors feel like? Instead of chasing trends, we built on Porsche’s core values: emotional connection, intuitive performance and timeless design. With three audiences in mind (first-time buyers, longtime owners and EV enthusiasts), we created a vision that blends systems thinking, storytelling and design.

Problem

How can Porsche evolve into the electric era without losing the emotional intensity, precision and heritage that define it? Decades of analog excellence meet the demands of digital innovation.

Solution

We reimagined Porsche’s EV interiors by blending tradition with innovation: intuitive, emotionally resonant interfaces that honor the brand’s legacy while embracing a connected, digital future.

Over 80 years of heritage has made Porsche more than just a car. It’s an icon of emotion, precision, and performance.

But as the world shifts to electric, a question emerges: can an EV truly feel like a Porsche? Can it carry the same intensity, the same soul, without the roar of the engine?

To begin, we needed to deeply understand the tension between heritage and innovation, and how to merge the two without compromise.

160+survey participants
30+interview participants
4design sprints
60+screens designed
30+user-testing participants
4rounds of iteration

Heritage vs. Innovation. Merging legacy with digital interactions.

Why don’t EVs feel like Porsche?

The app, in-car system and digital tools feel disjointed, eroding brand trust.

92% of EV owners plan to buy another electric vehicle
62% of users under 38 want their EV to feel “smart and connected”, anticipating needs without interruptions
71% of loyal owners fear tech will “interfere with the purity of driving”

How might we merge modern technology with Porsche’s analog soul?

How might we make technology disappear into the driving experience?

68%

preferred a mix of physical and digital controls, with critical functions kept physical for precision

42%

said full touch-based UIs made them feel distracted or unsure

Porsche Experience Center

Our visit to the Porsche Experience Center in Atlanta reinforced our core themes of Trust Through Touch and Heritage vs. Innovation.

Design Principles

01

Belonging over Status

Prioritizes connection over hierarchy: inclusivity, equality and user-centered design that fosters emotional connection and community.

02

Focus

Putting the driver first. Controls and info are placed to minimize distraction, like the Taycan’s curved display aligned to the driver’s view.

03

Timeless over Trend

Favors lasting, classic design over fleeting styles: relevance that endures over hype that fades.

04

Commitment over Convenience

A Porsche is built to last. A decades-long bond, not a passing trend: enduring quality, trust and timeless design.

05

Experience over Medium

It starts with the drive. Every choice, digital or physical, serves the driver first. Technology follows the experience.

06

Cultivating Tension

Heritage and innovation, analog and digital, sport and refinement. Tactile switches meet touchscreens in harmony.

Who we designed for

Three audiences, one Porsche feeling. Hover or tap to expand.

First Time Buyers: Younger professionals entering the Porsche world for the first time. They want innovation, luxury and performance, with digital ease and the tactile thrill of driving.
Legacy Owners: Loyal drivers with a deep appreciation for heritage and craftsmanship. Open to electric innovation as long as it honors the mechanical soul they trust.
EV Owners outside Porsche: Tech-forward EV drivers seeking more emotion, refinement and performance, ready for a driving experience that feels truly elevated.

RePilot

Award

Certificate winner, The Rookie Awards

RePilot was recognized with a certificate in The Rookie Awards, an international competition for emerging creatives.

RePilot is a retrofit, emotion-aware driving assistant that upgrades the car you already own. A small sensor kit, a dashboard display and gentle actuators use predictive AI, emotion recognition and real-time driving data to keep drivers focused, calm and aware. Unlike self-driving systems, the driver always stays in control. RePilot supports, it never takes over.

Problem

Drivers lack adaptive safety and awareness.

Most cars on the road today have no idea how their driver is feeling, and no way to help.

Opportunity

Empathy-driven retrofit enhances driving safety.

Bring emotion-aware support to existing cars, without asking anyone to buy a new one.

RePilot

Retrofit

Market scan
17 responses

Primary research: survey

I surveyed 17 drivers about car tech, trust in AI and what would make a retrofit worth it. Here is every question, broken down.

Q1

On a scale of 1–5, how comfortable are you with current car tech (GPS, cruise control, driver assist)?

1 (5.9%)1
2 (11.8%)2
3 (17.6%)3
2 (11.8%)4
9 (52.9%)5

52.9% rated their comfort a 5. People already trust the basics.

Q2

What makes you hesitant to trust a self-driving AI system?

It’s not reliable yetUnreliabilityTechnology malfunctions
Like to have controlCritical thinking skills that machines don’t have
UncomfortableAnxiousTrust
Sudden brake accidents

Answers grouped into four themes. Reliability and control came up most.

Q3

Would you like the ability to manually override AI actions in real time?

  • Yes 76.5%
  • Maybe 23.5%
  • No 0%

Nobody said no. Override became a core feature: Manual mode, always one tap away.

Q4

What would motivate you to choose a retrofit kit over buying a new car with these features?

Tech customization
11 (64.7%)
Cost savings
10 (58.8%)
Sustainability
6 (35.3%)
Emotional attachment to car
6 (35.3%)
Level of customization offered
1 (5.9%)

Customization beat even cost savings.

Most participants were very comfortable with existing features like GPS, cruise control and driver assist. But when it came to trusting self-driving AI, many hesitated: worries about reliability, malfunctions and sudden braking, and the discomfort of giving up control. Several said machines still lack the judgment people bring to driving.

When asked why they’d choose a retrofit over a new car, people pointed to tech customization (64.7%) and cost savings (58.8%), with sustainability and emotional attachment to their car close behind. That confirmed RePilot meets a real need: smart, supportive features for the car people already love, on their budget.

Usability testing

Prototype testing

6 drivers tried the Figma prototype on a tablet mounted in a parked car. Round 2 tested the fixes. Switch rounds to compare.

Understand the emotional state bar
50%

67%

83%

50%
Finish onboarding without help
67%
Finding 1

Emotion bar was unclear

Half the testers read the bar as a speed meter.

Change: Added a “Driver Emotional State” label, Relaxed / Focused / Stressed markers and a color shift.

Finding 2

Alerts were easy to miss

With music on, two testers missed the emergency-vehicle sound.

Change: The whole screen now gets a red border, a warning icon over the car, and music ducks automatically.

Finding 3

Settings felt buried

A long list made people scroll while driving.

Change: Rebuilt settings as a radial menu with large targets around “Profile”.

Finding 4

Too many choices at once

Onboarding asked for everything on one screen.

Change: Split into one question per screen with big chips and a progress arrow.

Dashboard

Ride along

The real dashboard frames, played as one drive: wake word, a stress moment, a song request and an emergency-vehicle alert. It plays on its own, or step through.

Award

Certificate winner, The Rookie Awards

RePilot was recognized with a certificate in The Rookie Awards, an international competition for emerging creatives.

My role

I led this project end to end: secondary research, a 17-person survey, driver interviews, personas, the information architecture, onboarding and dashboard UI, prototyping in Figma and usability testing.

What I learned

Designing for drivers means designing for divided attention. Every screen had to work in a glance, and the most important feature turned out to be the one that gives control back: manual override.

Why did I choose this project?

Menstrual health is something many people struggle to track. I wanted to work on something meaningful that could actually help people understand their cycles better. There’s still a lot of hesitation around the topic, and I think technology can make things easier and more accessible. This project felt like the right choice because it’s practical, personal, and has real impact.

About Floura

Ever wished you had a little helper to remind you about your period before it surprises you? Floura is your personal cycle companion: no more guessing or scribbling down dates. Floura helps you track your periods easily and stay connected with your health, helping you feel your best through every phase.

Problem statement

Many people struggle to track their menstrual cycles accurately, relying on memory or calendars and often missing predictions. Without a clear way to monitor patterns, symptoms, and lifestyle effects, they often feel unprepared and unsure about their health.

Possible solution

Floura makes it easy for women to track their cycles and stay on top of their health. It helps them stay prepared, understand their bodies, and build better habits. With no more guesswork or manual tracking, managing menstrual health feels effortless.

( Secondary research )

Desk research

  • I looked at how period tracking apps work and what people like or dislike about them.
  • This helps me understand what’s missing so I can make a better app.
  • I checked what features other apps have and what users really need.
  • With this information, I can create an app that’s easy to use and accurate.
  • This research helps me build something useful that actually helps people.

Competitive analysis

I chose Flo and Clue as my main competitors to analyze their strengths, weaknesses, and missing features. This analysis provided valuable insights.

Pros
  • Provides reminders for upcoming periods.
  • Allows users to manually log emotions and symptoms.
  • Tracks periods accurately.
  • Offers customizable period tracking (flow, symptoms, etc.).
  • Comprehensive health insights.
Cons
  • Lacks lifestyle recommendations.
  • Too many features are locked behind a paywall.
  • The login process is time-consuming.
  • Lacks a user-friendly design.
  • Poor user interface.
Pros
  • Provides reminders for upcoming periods.
  • Allows users to manually log emotions and symptoms.
  • Offers customizable period tracking (flow, pain, etc.).
  • Educational content.
Cons
  • Does not predict the next period.
  • Lacks lifestyle recommendations (diet, exercise, hydration).
  • No feedback messages.
  • Inaccurate predictions.
  • Limited symptom options.

What users are saying

Users struggle with missing reminders and limited symptom tracking. Editing period dates is impossible without reinstalling, and the removed weight-tracking feature frustrates many. Logging in is slow, and the app lacks helpful insights. The design also feels confusing, making tracking harder than it should be.

( Primary research )

Interview questions

16 questions I asked in my user interviews.

Show all 16 questions
  1. Can you tell me a little about yourself (age, daily routine, lifestyle)?
  2. Do you usually keep track of your monthly cycle? Why or why not?
  3. How do you feel when your period is about to start or ends?
  4. Have you ever had trouble remembering when your period will come?
  5. What are some things you like to know about your period (like flow, pain, mood)?
  6. Do you ever notice changes in your body before or during your period?
  7. Have you ever missed a period or had it come earlier or later than expected?
  8. Do you write down any details about your period (like dates, pain, emotions)? How?
  9. What kind of problems do you face during your period (pain, emotions, skin issues, etc.)?
  10. Do you usually talk to someone (like a friend, doctor, or parent) about your period?
  11. Do you do anything special to manage your symptoms (home remedies, rest, food)?
  12. Is it easy for you to understand your own cycle, or is it confusing sometimes?
  13. How would you like to feel more prepared or in control during your period?
  14. Is there anything you wish you had known earlier about your cycle or body?
  15. If someone could help make your period experience easier, what would you want help with?
  16. Do you think tracking your body or emotions during the month would be helpful? Why?
Insights derived from the interviews

Users struggle with missing reminders and limited symptom tracking. Editing period dates is impossible without reinstalling, and the removed weight-tracking feature frustrates many. Logging in is slow, and the app lacks helpful insights. The design also feels confusing, making tracking harder than it should be.

Problem statement

Many people, like students and working professionals, have busy lives and often forget to track their periods. This can lead to unexpected surprises, stress, and difficulty in understanding their cycle patterns. Some rely on memory, while others find tracking too complicated or time-consuming. They need a simple, easy-to-use way to keep track of their periods without extra effort, so they can feel more prepared and in control of their health.

How might we?

How might we create a simple and intuitive tool for people who struggle with tracking their periods and maintaining wellness, that they can easily use at home, work, or while traveling, to help them feel more prepared and reduce stress?

  • WHAT What do we want to achieve?
  • WHOM Who are we designing for?

  • WHY Why is this necessary / important?

CASE FILE, TRUE CRIME RING, CASE FILE, TRUE CRIME RING, CASE FILE, TRUE CRIME RING, CASE FILE, TRUE CRIME RING,

A true crime magazine where the design escalates with the crime.

Using four years of experience in Photoshop, Illustrator and InDesign, I designed CRIME., a complete magazine for my AP 2D Graphic Design Sustained Investigation. The issues move from minor crimes to the most serious ones, and the design grows with them.

Fonts, colors and perspective stay consistent, but every spread is designed around its featured crime. Bold headlines and eye-catching images pull readers in; muted color and shadowy imagery keep them in suspense.

Process film

From blank page to finished issue

A look at how CRIME. came together in Photoshop, InDesign and Illustrator.

Concept

The crime ladder

The investigation was built as a progression: ten crimes, from minor to the most severe. Drag the slider or tap a level to see how each spread answers its crime.

MinorSevere
Level 01 / 10

Illegal fingerprint business

Fingerprint swirls in mint green and a dropper under UV light: forensic, clinical, almost playful.

Design system

One system, many voices

Consistency came from type and color. Personality came from how each spread bent the rules.

MastheadCRIME.

A tall, high-contrast serif with a hard full stop. Reads like a newspaper of record.

Crime titlesARSON

A distressed, stamped red display face. Every crime gets the same treatment, so the series feels like case files.

SubheadsIS A HUGE CRIME

Thin, wide geometric caps. Quiet next to the loud titles, like a caption under evidence.

BodyLorem ipsum…

Dense, justified body text shaped into silhouettes, flames and columns, used as texture, not just copy.

Print

The printed issue

Five spreads from the print magazine. Pick one, or use the arrows.

Type as image

Body copy is shaped into silhouettes, columns and flames, so even the “lorem ipsum” becomes part of the illustration.

Repetition as tension

“Violence” and “Killer” repeat down the gutters like a pattern you can’t look away from.

Neon cut-outs

Glowing outlines pull subjects out of their scenes, a signature move across the series.

Digital

Taking it digital

The magazine continues online: the same masthead and red titles, adapted to phone, tablet and laptop layouts with navigation, social links and a subscribe bar.

Web template
CRIME.HomeOther magazinesSearch tags
TITLESUBHEAD

Subscribe to our online magazine now Apply

A reusable layout keeps every article familiar: masthead and nav on top, a stacked social rail on the left, the stamped red title, dense article text and a hero image that bleeds off the edge.

Campaign

Out in the world

A billboard brings the series to the street, using a calm sage background so the masthead and an open spread stand out at night.

My role

Concept, art direction, photo compositing, typography and layout for the full magazine: cover, print spreads, digital article templates and the billboard campaign.

What I learned

A strict system is what lets you break the rules. Because the masthead, red titles and black base never change, each spread could take big risks and still clearly belong to the same magazine.

Concept exploration

Illustration concepts

Before the final diagrams, I sketched and rendered 3D concepts that explain each product as a physical object. Pick a product, then flip between my sketch and the render.

ATOM 3D, Discover, Design, Deploy

A magnifying glass over the workflow

ATOM 3D follows three steps: Discovery maps workflows and finds intelligence gaps, Design co-creates the future state, and Deploy puts the ecosystem in place. The lens and building blocks show “looking closely, then rebuilding with intention.”

Record Ranger OS, Document intelligence

A machine that turns paper into data

Record Ranger takes in any P&C or medical document, then classifies, extracts and summarizes it, with human review before delivering clean, structured output. Messy files go in one side and tidy blocks come out the other.

AI Agents, Activation

A core that plugs into your systems

Structured data flows from Record Ranger into custom agents that plug into existing systems and automate decisions end to end. The glass panels show the agent connecting to each tool, while the client keeps full ownership of the agent IP.

Interactive concept

Point to Point

One graphic for the whole ecosystem, mixing 3D and flat elements. Each part is a touchpoint visitors can click to watch a demo or learn about that step. It started as sketches of a messy workflow becoming organized, layered intelligence.

An AI companion for pet care.

For Microsoft’s Generate 2024 workshop, we went to the Microsoft building in Atlanta, were given a theme, and designed a project to showcase to the Microsoft team. Our answer was Pawsitive: one app that keeps a pet’s profile and health records together, and uses AI to help owners when something seems wrong.

On site

A day at Microsoft

Generate 2024 took place inside Microsoft’s Atlanta office: we got our theme in the morning, built Pawsitive at these tables, and pitched it to the Microsoft team by the end of the day.

Research

Why pets need this

66%

of U.S. households own a pet (as of 2023). That’s 86.9 million homes.

Key insights

Owners struggle to understand their pet’s health conditions.

They want to care effectively at home.

They often miss early health risks.

Target audience

Pet owners who want to take the lead in understanding their pet’s situation, with AI as a helpful guide and professionals giving advice.

Unique value
TargetedEducationalAccessibleTrustworthy

The tool should be easy to navigate and understand, with educational content that helps owners learn more about their pet’s health.

Big buttons, one question per screen, plain language.

Chat, voice notes and photos instead of long forms.

Step 1

Open + guide

The app guides you to the data input section: video, sound, photos, breathing, a description, daily routine and habits, with instruction forms.

AI functionality

The AI analyzes the pet’s health data, looking for patterns and indicators of health conditions. It then uses that analysis to give targeted healthcare recommendations, helping owners make informed decisions about their pet’s health.

A smart collar that reads your pet’s temperature and heartbeat and syncs with the app, so the AI can run a basic checkup before a diagnosis.

Turning family shopping trips into a game.

At Kohl’s Emerging Talent Summit, our team was asked how Kohl’s could build loyalty with families. I led Group 3. Our answer was the Fam-Style Bundle: mix-and-match bundles built around family types, unlocked by a QR story game in the Kohl’s app and promoted with #KohlsFamily.

Competitive analysis

Where Kohl’s stands

Kohl’s already has the pieces: Kohl’s Cash, Sephora and Babies“R”Us partnerships, private label brands and an app. The opportunity is to make the app more interactive and turn shoppers into loyal “Kohl’s shoppers.”

  • Sephora + Babies“R”Us partnerships
  • Private label brands
  • Website + app
Opportunities

  • A more interactive app
  • Awareness of the brands Kohl’s carries
  • Creating a loyal “Kohl’s shopper”

Everyone bundles, but nobody makes it personal to a family.

e.g. Buy hot dogs, get free baked beans

Bundles named after family types make bundling feel natural and meaningful.

Promote bundles through archetypes like “Eco-Family Favorites,” with #KohlsFamily and #KohlsFamStyleBundle.

TikTok

Tutorial videos on how to play the in-app QR code game.

Influencers

2–3 creators with high engagement and different family dynamics play the game and shop bundles in store.

Commercials

Introduce families to the bundles: there is a bundle for every family.

Financial plan

Does it pay off?

Low-cost digital printing and QR signage: about $2k per store across 1,000 stores that all have Sephora. Move the sliders to test the plan.

5 years, 10% discount rate, $2M upfront
Revenue / year$540,000
NPV (5 yrs)$47,025
IRR10.9%

Positive NPV and an IRR above 10%: the plan is profitable.

“

Can a visitor quickly get from a question to the information or action they need?

The current experience has useful information but is overwhelming: visitors get lost and bounce off. The new landing page becomes the gateway that helps them understand, explore, search and act.
Six questions the page has to answer
  1. 01What is this place?
  2. 02Why is it significant?
  3. 03What can I see or do there?
  4. 04How do I plan a visit?
  5. 05How can I quickly find specific information?
  6. 06What information do I need before I go?
1.1The mountain

What Mount Fuji is, and why it matters

3776 m

Tallest mountain in Japan (12,389 ft)

~100 km

Southwest of Tokyo, between Yamanashi and Shizuoka

1707

Last eruption. Still active and monitored

2013

UNESCO World Heritage Site

What is Mount Fuji?

The tallest mountain in Japan, standing at 3,776 meters (12,389 feet). A volcano with a very symmetrical shape, about 100 km southwest of Tokyo, between Yamanashi and Shizuoka prefectures. Still active, but it has not erupted since 1707. Scientists continue to monitor it.

Why is it important?

An important religious and cultural symbol of Japan. People have climbed it for hundreds of years as pilgrimage. It inspired Hokusai and Hiroshige, whose artwork made Fuji recognizable around the world. In 2013, UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site for its religious and artistic importance.

What can I see or do? Tap a place

When should I go?

For climbing

Season is usually early July to early September. Winter climbing is dangerous: only experienced climbers with the right equipment.

JFMAMJJASOND
For seeing Fuji

Late fall through winter usually has the clearest skies. Morning is best: clouds often appear later in the day.

Cherry blossoms

Getting there from Tokyo

Kawaguchiko
About 2 hours from Shinjuku by train or bus
Hakone
About 85 minutes from Shinjuku by train
Fujinomiya
Shinkansen to Shin-Fuji, then a local bus
Gotemba
About 2 hours by express bus or train

You cannot take a train directly to the hiking trails. You usually need a shuttle bus or taxi to reach the 5th Stations.

Before you go

  • Weather & altitudeThe top can be very cold, even in summer, and weather changes quickly. Altitude sickness can happen: if you feel dizzy, sick or confused, stop and go back down.
  • Book earlySome trails require reservations and a climbing fee. Huts fill up quickly in July and August.
  • Follow the rulesStay on marked trails, use official bathrooms, take your trash. Avoid “bullet climbing” overnight without rest.
  • Check firstAlways check the weather, trail conditions and volcano warnings before climbing.

What to bring 0 / 11 packed
