2.1Content audit

29 pieces of content across 5 source types

I listed every piece of information a visitor needs, where it lives today, and what goes wrong. Filter and tap any card.

Officialfujisan-climb.jp (Yamanashi), FUJI NAVI app (Shizuoka), Japan Meteorological Agency, UNESCO
Tourismjapan.travel (JNTO), Fuji Five Lakes, Hakone and Fujinomiya tourism sites
Booking / ticketingAsoview, hut booking sites, bus and train operators
Guides / reviewsjapan-guide.com, blogs, Google Maps, TripAdvisor
SocialInstagram, YouTube, Reddit

What’s true

Potential problem

Visitor need

They search

What the audit shows

1Key facts are split across systems

A climber must piece together season, fee, registration, gate hours and huts from two prefectural systems, hut sites and blogs. A navigation problem more than a content gap.

2Websites often disagree or are out of date

Fees, daily limits and dates are different on different websites. Every fact should show when it was last updated and where it came from.

3Climbing and visiting are mixed together

Most visitors never climb, but the strongest content is about climbing.

4Accessibility, parking and live conditions have the least information

Many visitors need this information, but it is hard to find and often not trustworthy.

Three real websites, screen by screen

Key IA problems
  1. 1No visible global nav or search on desktop: everything hides behind the hamburger.
  2. 2All 11 pages sit in one long list with no groups, and the page names are confusing (like “Top” for the home page).
  3. 3Lots of repeats: the footer copies the menu, the same video shows 3 times in different languages, and page titles repeat.
  4. 4Climbers and sightseers are mixed together; off-season visitors get little direction.
  5. 5Real-time updates (volcano alerts, whether trails are open) are useful, but spread around and never explained.
IssueWorksImprove
01Home / hero41
  • Status-first heroLeading with “Mt. Fuji is currently closed” answers the #1 visitor question immediately.
  • Trail closures as a text wallFive closure lines in plain paragraphs; hard to scan which trail, which section, and when it reopens.
  • Competing CTAsTwo equal-weight buttons; off-season visitors aren’t told what to do next.
  • Nav hidden behind a hamburger on desktopNo visible global navigation or search.
  • Decorative vertical textA rotated label adds noise and competes with content.

ImproveStatus badge + next season opening date. Trail status as scannable chips. Persistent top nav with task-based groups + search.

02About section20
  • Brand mark takes a full viewportLarge logo + tagline push practical info (alerts, news) below the fold.
  • Vague label “About”Mission statement placed before useful content.

ImproveCollapse to one line under the hero. Prioritise conditions and planning content.

03Volcano info + News41
  • Live alert levelReal-time volcano status with a timestamp: high-value, trustworthy info.
  • No scale or meaning“Level 1” with no legend; users can’t tell if 1 is safe or severe.
  • Half-width box, empty columnWeather and trail status could live in the blank space.
  • Ambiguous bell bar“News” looks like a subscribe control but isn’t.
  • Long, bracket-heavy titlesPrefecture codes in brackets; no filters by trail or topic.

ImproveGroup into a “Current conditions” module (alert scale 1–5, weather, trail status). Add tag filters to News.

04Videos30
  • Same video ×3 languagesThree cards are one video in JP/EN/CN.
  • All body text styled as linksBold blue paragraphs; no hierarchy between title and description.
  • Language switch not usedAn EN switcher exists, yet every language still shows.

ImproveOne card per video, language follows the global switch. Group videos by topic: safety, routes, etiquette.

05Footer sitemap30
  • Awkward, inconsistent labels“About each trail” vs “About the Climbing Trail”; “Top” instead of “Home”.
  • Critical item not prioritised“Things you must know” sits in the same flat grid as “Video”.
  • Unlabeled logosPartner icons with no names or links explained.

ImproveGroup into Plan, On the mountain, Learn, Updates. Add contact, access and permit/fee links.

06Menu overlay30
  • No grouping or priorityScanning cost is high.
  • “What’s happening now” scatteredWarning/Volcano, News and Diary are all live info, but apart.
  • Missing essentialsNo search; no reservations, fees, access, weather or gear checklist.

ImproveCard sort into ~5 categories. Lead with “Plan your climb”. Add search in the menu.

07Mt. Fuji diary30
  • Title repeated“Mt. Fuji diary” in the hero and again in a bordered box.
  • Non-descriptive titles“Looking back… (3)(2)(1)”: users can’t tell posts apart.
  • Stale content signalLatest post is from 2025; no sign of update frequency.

ImproveDescriptive titles, topic tags, a filter and a “last updated” date.

08How to enjoy Mt. Fuji40
  • Tabs wrap to two rowsFive long tab labels; hard to see they’re one control.
  • A sentence as a tab label“It’s not just about climbing Mount Fuji! Recommended…”
  • Mixed audiencesTraining (climbers) sits next to nature/history (sightseers).
  • Text-heavyDense paragraphs; no images or checklists for training.

ImproveSplit “Prepare” (training, gear) from “Explore” (nature, culture, facilities). Short labels, anchor nav.

Show if it’s open first

A chip by the title says if the climbing season is open, and when it opens next.

A main menu plus one bar that jumps to every section.

Fee, daily limit, booking, closing hours and required gear in one box, said once.

Compare, don’t describe

Tables and cards for trails, routes and hotels, with distance to the trail start.

Fixes: stats written as long text

A two-day climb plan and a crowd calendar you can see at a glance.

2.2User Needs Matrix

Three visitors, three different first questions

F
First-time touristPrimary goal

Understand what to see and how to visit

Questions they might ask
What is Mt Fuji known for?Do I have to climb it to enjoy it?Where is the best place to see it?How long does it take from Tokyo?Will the mountain be visible when I go?
Potential frustrations
  • Dozens of “best spots” lists with no clear pick
  • Clouds hide the mountain and there is no live visibility check
  • Unclear whether climbing is possible on their dates
  • Train, bus and tour options are spread across many sites
Needs first
  • What it is and why it matters, in a few lines
  • Top viewpoints: Chureito Pagoda, Lake Kawaguchiko, Hakone
  • Getting there from Tokyo with time and cost (about 1 h 53 min by Fuji Excursion)
  • Best time of year and day to see it clearly
Needs later
  • Climbing rules, fee and huts, if they want to climb
  • Shrines and the Fujisan World Heritage Center (free entry)
  • Dining, lodging and day-trip tours
They might search for⌕ how to get to Mt Fuji from Tokyo⌕ best place to see Mt Fuji⌕ can I climb Mt Fuji⌕ Mt Fuji day trip⌕ is Mt Fuji visible today
L
Local visitorPrimary goal

Find events, exhibitions and activities

Questions they might ask
What is on this weekend or this season?Are the festivals free, and do I need tickets?Where can I park, and how crowded will it be?Which exhibitions or museums are open?Is there something new since my last visit?
Potential frustrations
  • Event dates change yearly and old listings stay online
  • Peak weekends and Golden Week are crowded, and the advice is buried
  • Parking fees and capacity are not shown
  • Event information is scattered across many listing sites
Needs first
  • Event calendar with dates, place and admission: Yoshida Fire Festival is fixed on Aug 26–27; Shibazakura runs mid-April to late May
  • Parking, roads and crowd levels, with peak days flagged
  • Opening hours for museums and exhibitions
  • Shuttle and last-bus times for event days
Needs later
  • Overnight lodging for big events (August books up a month or more ahead)
  • Background and history of each festival
  • Tours and guided activities
They might search for⌕ Fuji Shibazakura Festival dates⌕ Yoshida Fire Festival schedule⌕ Lake Kawaguchiko fireworks⌕ Fujisan World Heritage Center hours⌕ Mt Fuji parking
I
International travelerPrimary goal

Plan transport, tickets, language and logistics

Questions they might ask
How do I get there without speaking Japanese?Which train or bus, and how much is it?Do I need a seat reservation, and does my JR Pass work?Where do I leave my luggage?Do I need a reservation to climb?
Potential frustrations
  • The JR Pass covers only Shinjuku to Otsuki on the Fuji Excursion
  • Two climbing systems: a website and an app
  • Resellers and blogs show conflicting fares and dates
  • Timetables and shuttles change by season
Needs first
  • Transport with fares, times and booking steps: Fuji Excursion about ¥4,130 and 1 h 53 min, highway bus about ¥2,200
  • Climbing registration: fujisan-climb.jp for Yoshida, the FUJI NAVI app for the Shizuoka trails
  • Information in English with one clear first step
  • Luggage storage and station facilities
Needs later
  • Events and festivals during the stay
  • Trail and shrine etiquette, trash rules
  • Dining and lodging with English menus
They might search for⌕ Fuji Excursion ticket⌕ does JR Pass cover Mt Fuji⌕ Mt Fuji climbing reservation 2026⌕ Tokyo to Kawaguchiko bus⌕ Mt Fuji luggage storage

    3.2Taxonomy

    Labeling principles and the main navigation

    Research 01Use the words visitors search

    People search with everyday words and real names, like “can I climb Mt Fuji” and “Fuji Excursion ticket,” so the labels use those same words.

    Research 02One term per concept

    Sources called the same ¥4,000 charge an entry fee, hiking fee, trail fee, permit and admission fee. The site says “Climbing fee” everywhere and search maps the rest.

    Rule 03Navigation names the place, buttons name the action

    Nav says where you are going (Climb Fuji). Buttons say what happens next (Reserve your climb).

    Rule 04No vague labels

    “Information”, “More”, “Resources” and “Other” are banned. A label that could hold anything hides things.

    Rule 05Say what is on the other side

    “Check conditions today” beats “Today.” “See fares and times” beats “Learn more.”

    Rule 06Short enough to translate

    Labels stay near three words so the EN/JP switch does not break the header.

    3.3Labeling system

    Five important labels, compared and explained

    Nav label
    Climb Fuji
    • HikingToo broad. Visitors also hike lake trails, and sources say “climb.”
    • TrailsHides the rules and booking climbers need first.
    • ResourcesVague. Banned by the principles.

    Why this wordingThe official websites say “climb,” and people search “can I climb Mt Fuji.” Giving climbing its own label keeps it apart from sightseeing.

    Nav label
    Getting Here & Access
    • Plan Your TripToo broad. It would hold everything and hide transport again.
    • TransportationLeaves out parking and accessibility.
    • Visitor InformationVague. Banned by the principles.

    Why this wording“How do I get there?” is the first question travelers ask. “Access” covers parking and accessibility too. Two of three card-sort users made a “Getting there” pile.

    Term
    Climbing fee
    • Entry or admission feeSounds like a ticket to a place.
    • Trail or hiking fee“Hiking” clashes with “Climb Fuji.”
    • PermitSuggests a document to carry; the real step is registration plus payment.

    Why this wordingWebsites use five names for the same ¥4,000 charge. “Fee” makes it clear you pay, and “climbing” matches the section. Searching any other name still finds it.

    Call to action
    Reserve your climb
    • Book nowVague. It does not say what is being booked.
    • RegisterUsed for the FUJI NAVI app, but unclear for the website route.
    • Buy ticketWrong for a fee plus registration, and wrong for hut stays.

    Why this wording“Reserve” is a word people know from trains and hotels; “your climb” says what is booked. The button shows simple steps for each trail.

    Nav label
    Conditions & Safety
    • TodayUnclear what is inside. A date is not a topic.
    • AlertsLeaves out forecasts and health advice.
    • WeatherMisses the volcano alert level and altitude health.

    Why this wording“Conditions” means what is happening now, and “Safety” means how to stay safe. Together they answer one question: “Should I go today?”

    Calls to action Hover to swap the old label for the new one

    Climb Fuji checklist
    Book nowReserve your climb

    Names the object and matches the reservation systems.

    Hut card
    AccommodationBook a mountain hut

    A verb for the action; a noun has no next step.

    Trail comparison
    Learn moreCompare trails

    Tells climbers they will see four trails on the same fields.

    Getting Here fares
    Click hereSee fares and times

    Says what is behind the link.

    Train option
    BookReserve a seat

    The Fuji Excursion needs a seat reservation, so the label says so.

    Home live strip
    TodayCheck conditions today

    A verb and a time frame answer “should I go today?”

    Events list
    MoreSee this season’s events

    Scopes the list so locals know it is current.

    Maps and venues
    MapGet directions

    Action first; a bare “Map” does not say what happens.

    Supporting labels

    TrustOfficial sourceLast updated: dateVerified for 2026
    StatusReservation requiredFree admissionFee appliesClosed in winter
    Season and timeSeason: Jul 1 to Sep 10Best in the morningPeak crowds: weekends
    AccessStep-free routeStairs: about 400Access: not documented yet

    Cross-links between sections

    Why this structure

    UsersThree doors in, one set of pages

    Three visitor types have different first steps. Home shortcuts open the same pages in a different order, so nothing is duplicated.

    AuditOne section page for the booking rules

    Climbing rules were split across two systems and many blogs. Before you book holds all five rule pages together.

    AuditLive information has one home and many links

    Weather, visibility and volcano alerts live in Conditions & Safety and are cross-linked where decisions happen.

    RuleThree levels, three clicks

    Section pages double as the secondary navigation. Detail pages stay one click below, so no page is buried.

    3.6Landing-page hierarchy

    Ten blocks in visitor order

    Tap a block to see the question it answers. Pick a visitor to see what they need first.

    Above the foldBlocks 1, 2, 3

    Where am I, and can I find my thing? Visitors decide in seconds whether the site helps.

    Core contentBlocks 4, 5, 6, 7

    How do I do the thing I came for? Each block is one visitor task.

    SupportingBlocks 8, 9, 10

    What else do I need to feel sure? Context and reassurance, never in the way of a fare or a rule.

    end of first screen

    What is inside

    Maps to

    Audit items

    The reasoning, block by block

    1User needsTitle, short intro and main buttons

    The big button says “Plan your visit” because most people never climb. Climbing gets the smaller second button.

    2Website researchSearch comes right after the top

    Fuji info is spread across many websites, and many people come with one question.

    3User needsA button for each type of visitor

    Same content in the order each visitor needs it, so nothing is repeated.

    4Website researchA strip that shows today’s conditions

    Weather, visibility and volcano alerts in one place, so visitors can tell if today is a good day.

    5Page orderEverything important fits on the first screen

    Even someone who never scrolls can still plan, search or decide not to go.

    6UsersPlan comes before sights

    Getting there decides the trip. Fares appear side by side because the audit found them spread across many sites.

    7AuditParking and accessibility get cards, not footer links

    Access, parking and shuttles were the thinnest content.

    8UsersSights for everyone sit before the climbing hub

    Explore keeps four free, permit-free ideas ahead of the booking rules.

    9AuditOne hub for the climbing rules, season status first

    In October the most useful fact is that the season has ended, so the status leads and the button waits below.

    10OrderClimb Fuji is mid-page, not first

    The highest-stakes task, but the smaller audience.

    11UsersEvents come before history

    Locals look for events first; dated items keep the section current.

    12UsersMeaning follows action

    The longer story is lower so it never slows a fare or a rule, but it stays one click from the hero.

    13AuditHelp is a block, not a dead end

    FAQs answer the repeat questions, and a person is one button away.

    14RuleThe footer repeats the six nav labels and trust links

    So a visitor who scrolled to the end can still go anywhere.

    Ordering decisions

    Today strip goes third, above Plan Your VisitRejected: Plan Your Visit directly after search

    A decision to go or not comes before a decision about how. The strip is short.

    Plan Your Visit before Explore FujiRejected: Sights first, as in the example order

    Fuji is hours from Tokyo and the climb season is short. First-time and international visitors need getting there first.

    Climb Fuji sits mid-page, after ExploreRejected: Climbing right under the hero

    Climbers are a minority and reach the hub from the hero link, nav and search.

    What’s Happening before Why It MattersRejected: History before events, as in the example

    Locals look for events first. The hero already carries a one-line “what is it”.

    Help and FAQ stays on the pageRejected: Moving it entirely to the footer

    Access and safety facts were thin and hard to find. A visible block keeps them reachable.

    Test with a tree test and scroll mapsRejected: Not decided yet: all ordering is a hypothesis

    Run a first-click test and watch whether visitors scroll past block 4.

      What decides which result shows first

      Does it help them do what they want?
      35%
      Is it official and up to date?
      25%
      Does the page name match the search?
      20%
      What kind of page is it?
      10%

      Moves up: updated for this year, climbing pages in season, pages with every detail filled in. Moves down: old rules from past years, duplicate pages, articles when someone wants to book or pay. These percentages are my starting guess.

      Filters for “festival”

      Filters only appear when there are lots of results: “parking” finds 3, so no filters; “festival” finds 8+. Picked filters show as chips with “Clear all”. Dates show the next time each event happens.

      Content typeIncluded

      Splits when from where, so visitors pick the question they have.

      When (next occurrence)Included

      Events recur. Visitors plan by season, not by publish date.

      AreaIncluded

      Fuji Five Lakes, Hakone and Fujinomiya are different trips.

      Cost: freeIncluded

      A budget decision, one click.

      Access: step-freeIncluded

      Decides whether a place is possible at all for some visitors.

      Audience: groups or schoolsLeft out

      No group programs are documented yet. A filter with nothing behind it adds noise.

      LanguageLeft out

      The EN and JP switch already changes the whole page.

      Author or date publishedLeft out

      Nobody decides a visit by who wrote a page.

      Content type: history or articlesLeft out

      Too few items. They live under Discover.

      Price range sliderLeft out

      Only two cost states matter: free or fee.

      • A real person is always one button away.
      • Empty searches are saved, so the team knows which pages to add. It also fixes typos: “fuji excurson” → Fuji Excursion.

      5.3User testing

      Testing with three people

      Five realistic scenarios, one per page area.

      1. 1You’re a first-time traveler with one free day in Tokyo. Show me how you’d figure out whether visiting Fuji is worth it.
      2. 2You’re planning a trip with friends next August, none of you have hiked a big mountain, and you want the summit. Show me how you’d find out what to prepare.
      3. 3It’s October, you’re in Japan, and the climbing season is over. Show me how you’d find what you can still see or do.
      4. 4You’ve booked your climb and you’re packing tonight. Show me where you’d look for the gear you need.
      5. 5It’s the night before your climb and the weather looks windy. Show me how you’d check whether you should still go.
      “I can read English, but my parents can’t. The site only has English and Japanese.”
      International travelerLed to → More languages
      “There’s so much in the search area. I don’t know what I’m searching or what the results are.”
      Young first-time visitorLed to → A clearer, color-coded search
      “I couldn’t find where gear lives. The menu order felt random and the sitemap table was hard to follow.”
      Experienced hikerLed to → A visual sitemap and a better menu order
      5.4Before / after

      Four improvements I made

      01More languages

      The site only offered English and Japanese.

      I added more languages, so more international visitors can read it.

      02A visual sitemap

      The sitemap was a table, which was hard to read.

      I reorganized it into a visual map, so you can see how pages connect.

      03A clearer search

      The search area was crowded and had no clear structure.

      I reorganized it and color-coded the sections, so people understand what they are searching.

      04A better menu order

      The menu items were not in a helpful order.

      I reorganized the menu bar so items follow the order visitors need them.

      Restaurants throw out food every day while pantries run short. What if the pantry asked first?

      FoodBridge connects three people around the same food: a donor with surplus, a volunteer driving home anyway, and a coordinator who knows exactly what her community can use. One platform, three different jobs.

      Team: Valeria Múnera, Naza Mgbahurike and Yashi. I worked across all three roles, the donor, the driver and the coordinator, as well as the journey map, sitemap, handoffs and permissions.

      Context

      Why the food gets thrown away, who already tries to fix it, and the three people we designed for.

      2.1The problem

      Surplus everywhere, pantries short

      2.4Key takeaways

      What the research changed

      1. 01Sort by expirationAlmost half the surplus is produce, and it goes bad fast.
      2. 02Tell donors they’re coveredFederal law protects good-faith food donations. We can say it next to verification in onboarding.
      3. 03Make logging quickGoodr saw airport restaurant staff writing leftovers on receipts. Scanning solves that.
      4. 04Give donors proofPounds and meals, ready for taxes, in the Data tab.
      5. 05Start from the needNeither competitor lets nonprofits post what they need first. That’s our angle.

      We flipped who starts a donation

      2. 2Tashaaccepts, or says no

      One approval, not two

      Before, Rosa offered and Tasha could still say no. Now Tasha checks the food before she asks, so almost nothing gets rejected.

      Inventory earns its place

      Rosa’s inventory is what Tasha browses. That gives Rosa a real reason to keep scanning products and dates.

      Delight

      One improvement for each role, in the final app.

      5.1Final app

      One improvement for each role

      The final hi-fi screens for the coordinator, the donor and the driver, all built on the same shared structure. Pick a role, then tap a step or let it play.

      Restock before you run out

      Before

      The coordinator has to notice when something runs low, go browse donors, build a request item by item, and check fridge space and timing by hand.

      After

      FoodBridge spots what’s running low and suggests a request from a nearby donor, already filled and checked. The coordinator reviews it and slides to send. When the food arrives, needs update on their own.

      How the IA makes it possible

      Needs, inventory, and donor inventory are connected. Received food updates inventory, inventory updates needs, and needs rank what donors have. Receiving hours and the donor’s usual availability are both stored, so the pickup time can be matched automatically.

      Interactions

      The running low card sits at the top of Home. The suggested request opens as a sheet with the same slide to send used across the app. The dashed bar shows what a delivery will cover before it arrives, and the needs bars move after check-in.

      1 / 12
      Main flow
      Edge cases

      Confirm a request in one swipe

      Before

      A request comes in during a busy shift. The donor has to open it, look up what they have, type quantities and dates, pick a time, write instructions, and then wonder if anyone is actually coming.

      After

      The request shows up already filled from the donor’s inventory and profile. They check it, slide to confirm, and then watch the driver come to them in real time, without leaving Home.

      How the IA makes it possible

      Inventory, usual availability, and pickup instructions are saved once, in Products and Profile. The coordinator requests items from that inventory, so the request already knows quantities and expiration dates. Donation status is one shared object, so the same live card shows up on Home, in Active, and in notifications.

      Interactions

      A push banner drops in when a request arrives. The request opens as a sheet on top of Home, so the donor never loses their place. Slide to confirm prevents accidental taps during a shift. The live card and the map update on their own, and the screen changes when the driver arrives.

      1 / 11
      Main flow
      Edge cases

      Runs that fit the drive you’re already making

      Before

      A run offer shows two addresses. The driver has to work out how far it really is, if it fits in their car, and if the food will be ready when they get there. At the door they still have to find someone and say they arrived.

      After

      Drivers say where they’re already going, and FoodBridge shows runs that fit that drive. The offer says how many minutes it adds, how big the load is, and if the food is packed. The app notices when they arrive, and the checklist is already there.

      How the IA makes it possible

      The donor’s inventory gives the load size. The pickup window and instructions come from the donor profile, and the coordinator’s receiving hours set the drop-off deadline. Because these live in shared objects, the run offer can answer every question before the driver accepts.

      Interactions

      Runs on my way is one toggle. The offer opens as a sheet with a route preview. Slide to accept and slide to confirm pickup work the same as in the donor app. Arrival is detected by location, so the screen changes on its own.

      It started on paper

      5.3What changed

      Most of it came from mapping the handoffs as a group, and from critique

      1The model

      Tasha asks and Rosa confirms, instead of Rosa offering. Match % became the number of items requested.

      2The map

      Inventory step, notifications at every handoff, two exceptions, and one status vocabulary on every screen.

      3The structure

      A shared layer for what all three roles use, and a permissions table for who can change what.

      4The experience

      Onboarding, a live map, one improvement per role, cancel confirmations, and the class personas everywhere.

      Interactions and usability

      • Every commitment uses the same slide to confirm, and a tap works too.
      • Sheets open on top of the current screen, so people never lose their place.
      • Every commitment can be canceled, with a confirmation that says who gets told.
      • Every flow ends on a screen that reflects what just happened.
      • Touch targets are at least 44 px, and gray text was darkened so it passes contrast.

      Interior Design 3D Internship

      Vijayawada, India
      Main Role3D Design Intern
      MentorPavan Kumar
      Tools3ds Max, Hand sketching
      Project TypeResidential Interiors
      Sketch vs. render →Explore the TV stand →

      Residential interiors, from pencil to photoreal.

      During an internship in Vijayawada, India, designed alongside Pavan Kumar, I took rooms from hand-drawn perspective sketches to full 3D renders in 3ds Max: foyers, bedrooms, a study, and custom furniture like a child’s bedroom TV stand.

      The internship

      My story

      Before I opened 3ds Max, I spent my first weeks on site. Scroll through how the internship unfolded.

      1. Week 1Meeting the client

        The home belonged to a family in Vijayawada building a new flat: a couple, their young son and a grandparent who lives with them. I sat in on the first meeting with Pavan Kumar and took notes on how they actually live: where guests are received, where the kids study, how much storage they need.

      2. Week 1–2Going to the sites

        I visited the flat while it was still bare concrete, plus two other homes Pavan’s team was finishing. I measured rooms, photographed window positions and electrical points, and watched how the carpenters, painters and false-ceiling crews worked.

      3. Week 2Learning from the workers

        The site carpenters showed me how veneer is pressed onto plywood, why duco paint needs several coats and sanding, and how gypsum ceilings are framed. Talking to them changed my designs: I stopped drawing details that looked good but couldn’t actually be built on site.

      4. Week 3Material markets

        We visited laminate, tile and hardware showrooms to compare finishes, prices and lead times, and brought samples back to show the client.

      5. Week 3–4Sketching the rooms

        I drew every room in two-point perspective by hand so the client could react quickly before we committed to 3D.

      6. Week 4–6Modeling + rendering

        I built the approved spaces in 3ds Max, matched real material samples, set up lighting and rendered the final views the client used to sign off.

      Client

      The brief

      What the family asked for, and what I took from seeing the site.

      Warm, but easy to clean

      Vijayawada is hot, humid and dusty. Surfaces had to be glossy or sealed so they wipe down easily.

      Storage everywhere

      Built-in wardrobes, drawers under TV units and display niches so nothing sits on the floor.

      Kid-friendly

      Rounded edges, durable finishes and a TV wall for the son’s room that can grow with him.

      Light that sets a mood

      Cove lighting and spotlights so each room feels finished in the evening, not just under a tube light.

      Field work

      On site

      A TV stand for a child’s bedroom

      Practical and playful: storage for games, DVDs and cables, spotlit niches for small figurines, and rounded edges and durable finishes to make it kid-friendly. Tap the numbers.

      1Frosted glass backgroundSoft, even glow behind the TV.2Round display nichesSpotlit shelves for figurines and photos.3Glass shelves + spotlightsLight from above, nothing to bump into.4Wooden ledgeRounded edges, kid-safe.5Drawers in white ducoStorage for games, DVDs and cables.

      My role

      Site visits and measurements, client notes, materials research, perspective sketching, 3D modeling, materials and lighting in 3ds Max, and custom furniture design, working with Pavan Kumar.

      What I learned

      Standing on site taught me more than any software. Seeing how carpenters and painters actually build things made my designs more realistic, and lighting turned out to be what made each room feel finished.

      Watch the animation →Take it apart →

      A quadcopter modeled, assembled and animated from scratch.

      A camera drone I designed to practice surface modeling and motion. The body is one smooth surface in a deep merlot, with clear five-blade props and a tilting camera underneath. I modeled every part in SolidWorks, then brought the assembly into KeyShot for materials, lighting and animation.

      KeyShot animation
      Renders

      Every angle

      Studio renders straight out of KeyShot. Switch views.

      Exploded view

      Take it apart

      The full assembly, exploded. Click a number to see what each part does.

      1. 1
        Prop capsDomed caps lock each propeller to its motor shaft.
      2. 2
        Five-blade propsClear, swept blades: more lift at lower speed, so it runs quieter.
      3. 3
        Brushless motorsFour motors drop straight into the arm pods.
      4. 4
        Top windowGlass panel over the flight controller and status lights.
      5. 5
        Upper shellOne surfaced body; the arms flow out of the center with no hard joints.
      6. 6
        Motor bushingsRings that seat each motor and soak up vibration.
      7. 7
        Lower shellCloses the body and forms the motor pods.
      8. 8
        Camera mount plateScrews to the underside and carries the camera hinge.
      9. 9
        Camera moduleTilts on a two-lug hinge to frame shots in flight.
      Detail

      The camera module

      Four parts, one hinge. The housing’s two lugs let the camera tilt.

      HousingTwo lugs with holes make the tilt hinge.Lens ringGloss black bezel that threads onto the housing.LensFront element.Sensor pinLocates the lens stack inside the housing.
      Process

      How I made it

      From sketch-level surfaces to an animated render.

      SolidWorksSurface modeling

      Built the body as lofted and boundary surfaces so the arms blend smoothly into the center, then thickened it into upper and lower shells.

      SolidWorksAssembly + motion

      Assembled props, motors, shells and camera with mates, then ran a motion study to check the props spin clear and the camera tilts freely.

      KeyShotMaterials + lighting

      Matte merlot plastic, clear props, gloss black lens and brushed metal, lit in a soft white studio.

      KeyShotAnimation

      Camera moves, turntable and exploded-view animation, rendered out to the film at the top of this page.

      Side Project, Industrial Design

      Travel Stack

      Spring 2024
      Main RoleProduct Designer
      ProductTravel mug + 2 cups
      MaterialsPlastic, wood handles
      Made inBlender, start to finish
      Meet the personas →See the final poster →

      The ultimate travel mug for tea and coffee lovers.

      Travel Stack is a travel mug with two attachable cups at the bottom and detachable wooden handles, so you can pull the cups out and share your drink with friends and family on the go. Durable plastic for daily travel, eco-friendly wooden handles for a comfortable grip. I modeled, textured and rendered the whole thing in Blender.

      The design

      A big cup for a large amount of coffee. Two smaller cups fit into the main tumbler and come out when you need them. Strong, safe materials like stainless steel or BPA-free plastic keep drinks hot or cold for a long time, and each cup has a secure lid to prevent spills.

      What it’s good for

      Carry multiple drinks on a trip or a commute. Share with friends or family without extra cups. Keep coffee hot and tea warm for hours.

      Who it’s for

      Anyone always on the move. Different drinks at your desk. Hikes, picnics and other outdoor days. People who enjoy both coffee and tea.

      Side Project, Industrial Design

      Dash Electric Scooter

      Winter 2025
      Main RoleProduct Designer
      FocusErgonomics
      ToolsSolidWorks, KeyShot
      Project TypeConcept + renders
      See the ergonomics →See the poster →

      An electric scooter shaped around the rider.

      Dash is a commuter e-scooter where every curve comes from the body: one flowing S-shaped stem, swept grips, a speed readout right in your line of sight and a wide, sculpted deck. Modeled in SolidWorks and rendered in KeyShot in matte black, copper and red.

      Research

      Where riders hurt

      Before shaping anything, I looked at how people stand, grip and look on today’s scooters. Four problems kept coming up.

      01Wrist strain

      Straight, thin bars bend the wrist back on long rides and pass every bump into the hands.

      02Back + neck

      Fixed, upright stems make taller riders hunch and shorter riders reach.

      03Foot fatigue

      Narrow flat decks force one stance; feet go numb on longer commutes.

      04Glance + go

      Speed displays sit low on the stem, so riders look down and away from the road.

      Ergonomics

      Designed around the body

      Every part of the form answers one of those problems. Click a number.

      1. 1
        Swept handlebarGrips angle back slightly so the wrist stays neutral instead of bending, the same idea as an ergonomic mouse.
      2. 2
        Speed display in the line of sightThe 48 MPH readout sits on top of the stem, so a quick glance down keeps the road in view.
      3. 3
        S-curve stemThe stem bends forward, then back over the front wheel, bringing the grips closer to the body so riders stand tall instead of leaning.
      4. 4
        Second support strutA brace from the stem to the deck stiffens the frame and takes load off the hands over rough ground.
      5. 5
        Wide sculpted deckThe deck widens where the feet land and dips slightly in the middle, so riders can stand staggered or side by side.
      6. 6
        Wrap-around fenderA full fender with a clear guard keeps spray off legs and shoes.
      7. 7
        Large tiresBigger wheels roll over cracks and curbs more smoothly, so less vibration reaches the body.
      Anthropometrics

      Sizing to people

      Key dimensions came from body measurements, so most adults fit without adjusting.

      Grip Ø≈ 32 mm

      Fits the 5th–95th percentile hand in a full power grip.

      Grip width≈ 55–60 cm

      About shoulder width, so arms stay relaxed and elbows soft.

      Grip height≈ 100 cm

      Near wrist height when standing, for a straight-arm, upright posture.

      Deck width≈ 18 cm

      Room for a staggered stance and a shoe up to about US 13.

      Deck height≈ 9 cm

      Low enough to step on and off without lifting the knee high.

      Posture

      Stand tall, arms soft.

      The S-curve brings the grips back toward the rider and up to about wrist height, so the spine stays straight and the elbows relaxed instead of locking out or hunching forward.

      Fit range

      Who it fits

      I designed for the middle 90% of adult riders, from a 5th-percentile woman to a 95th-percentile man. Drag to see how the bar height feels at each size.

      150 cm, 4′11″190 cm, 6′3″
      Rider height167 cm
      Wrist height (standing)≈ 82 cm
      Elbow bend at the grips≈ 20°
      FitComfortable
      15–30°elbow bend

      Soft arms absorb bumps instead of the shoulders.

      ±10°wrist from neutral

      The swept bar keeps wrists close to straight on long rides.

      3–5 meyes ahead

      An upright stance keeps the rider looking at the road, not the deck.

      ≤ 10 cmstep-on height

      A low deck means no high knee lift at every stop.

      Process

      From line drawing to render

      The first wireframe sketch set the single-stem silhouette.

      ResearchRiding pain points

      Looked at how riders stand, grip and look on existing scooters, and where discomfort builds up on longer rides.

      ErgonomicsBody first

      Used anthropometric ranges for hand size, shoulder width and standing height to set grip size, bar width and deck size.

      SolidWorksModel the frame

      Swept the single curved stem, then built the deck, strut, fenders, wheels and grips around it.

      KeyShotRender + brand

      Matte black with copper rims and red accents, the vertical DASH wordmark on the stem, and a top-down poster.
